title: The Photon and the Atom

cards.h: The theory that broke Newton's world
cards.b:
Around 1900, classical physics could not explain why a hot poker glows the colours it does, why atoms do not collapse, or why shining light on metal knocks out electrons. The fix needed a radical idea: energy comes in tiny packets, called quanta.

This idea started quantum mechanics, the theory behind chemistry, lasers, computers and the chips in your phone.

Hot objects glow with a spectrum that classical physics could not explain. Max Planck found in 1900 that the curve fits if light is emitted in lumps of energy:

Planck's relation

E = h x f

f is the frequency and h is Planck's constant, 6.63 x 10 to the power -34 joule second. Higher frequency, bigger lump. Planck thought it a mathematical trick; it was the first hint of a new physics.

Shine light on a metal and electrons can be knocked out. Surprises: below a certain frequency no electrons come out, however bright the light. Above it, they come at once, and brighter light gives more electrons, not faster ones.

Einstein explained in 1905: light itself is made of particles, photons, each with energy hf. One photon knocks out one electron:

Photoelectric equation

kinetic energy of electron = h f - (work function)

He won the 1921 Nobel Prize for this, not for relativity.

Rutherford's atom (1911) has electrons orbiting a tiny nucleus, but classical physics said they should spiral in and crash. In 1913 Niels Bohr proposed that electrons can occupy only certain energy levels and radiate only when jumping between them.

For hydrogen: E(n) = -13.6 eV divided by n squared. A jump emits a photon with energy equal to the gap, giving the sharp coloured lines of atomic spectra. Every element has its own fingerprint, so we can read the chemistry of distant stars.

If light waves can act like particles, perhaps particles act like waves. Louis de Broglie suggested in 1924:

de Broglie wavelength

wavelength = h / (m v)

For an electron the wavelength is tiny but real, and electrons were seen to diffract in 1927. This is wave-particle duality. Electron microscopes use electron waves to see far smaller details than light can.

Werner Heisenberg (1927) showed we cannot know both position and momentum precisely at the same time: the product of their uncertainties is at least about h divided by 4 pi. It is not about clumsy instruments; it is built into nature.

Erwin Schrodinger's equation (1926) describes electrons by a wave function whose square gives the probability of finding the particle somewhere. Quantum physics predicts chances, not certainties.

cards.h: Energy of a photon and photoelectric emission
cards.b:
A handy rule: E (in eV) = 1240 / wavelength (in nm). For green light of 550 nm, E = 1240 / 550 = 2.25 eV.

Sodium has a work function of about 2.3 eV. Red light at 700 nm has 1.77 eV: no electrons, however bright. Blue light at 400 nm has 3.1 eV, so electrons emerge with energy 3.1 - 2.3 = 0.8 eV.

Hydrogen jump n = 3 to 2: 3.4 - 1.5 = 1.9 eV, wavelength 1240 / 1.9 = 650 nm, the red line.

• 'Electrons orbit like tiny planets.' Bohr's picture is a useful stepping stone; real electrons are spread-out clouds of probability.
  • 'Brighter light always gives faster photoelectrons.' Brightness gives more electrons; only higher frequency gives faster ones.
  • 'Uncertainty is about measuring badly.' It is a basic property of nature.

S. N. Bose's 1924 work, treating photons as indistinguishable particles, gave the correct counting for light quanta and launched Bose-Einstein statistics. Particles that follow it, such as photons and the Higgs, are called bosons in his honour.

C. V. Raman's 1928 effect is a direct sign of the photon: a photon loses or gains a bit of energy when it hits a molecule, appearing at a shifted colour. Meghnad Saha's 1920 equation links atomic energy levels to the temperature of stars.

• Energy comes in quanta: E = hf (Planck 1900).
  • Photons explain the photoelectric effect (Einstein 1905).
  • Atoms have discrete levels; jumps produce spectral lines (Bohr 1913).
  • Matter has a wavelength h/mv; the uncertainty principle limits what we can know.

Think about it

1. Why can a dim blue light eject electrons while a bright red light cannot?
2. Why does each element have its own line spectrum?
